source: Klutmann et al. (2026) Visualizing cognitive processes in medical education: forward and backward reasoning in a digital family medicine assessment
finding: Year-5 students recorded their reasoning on exam items. Forward reasoning (from stem data) was used more than backward reasoning (from answer options). High scorers used both more than low scorers.
numbers: N=210 (WS22/23 95 of 97, SS23 115 of 115). 87% of answers coded as clinical reasoning. FR>BR: p=0.006 and p<0.001. High vs low performers: OR 3.33 (95% CI 2.38-4.49) for FR, OR 2.67 (1.67-4.26) for BR.
limits: Self-report text boxes after answering, not live think-aloud. MCQ exam, not real patients. Here FR/BR mean stem-first vs options-first, a different meaning from Patel and Groen.
agent_relevance: Forward reasoning here means generating a hypothesis before seeing options. Cheap analogue for an agent: commit to a hypothesis from the data before reading candidate answers.

source: Klutmann et al. (2026) item-type and feedback results
finding: Backward reasoning rose on hard diagnostic items and on follow-up items. Formative feedback did not change reasoning type.
numbers: FR share 98.9% on a factual item vs 66.7% on a diagnostic item; BR 1.1% vs 33.3%. Feedback: chi2=3.38, p=0.281. Follow-up questions: BR OR 2.49 (2.29-2.84) in SS23 but no effect in WS22/23 (p=0.299).
limits: Two cohorts disagree on the follow-up effect, so it is fragile. Item mix was unbalanced.
agent_relevance: Strategy shifts with task difficulty and prompt structure, so a scaffold should not assume one fixed direction of reasoning.

source: Coderre, Mandin, Harasym, Fick (2003) Diagnostic reasoning strategies and diagnostic success
finding: Think-aloud study in gastroenterology. Pattern recognition and scheme-inductive reasoning gave higher odds of a correct diagnosis than hypothetico-deductive reasoning. Expertise and case content were independent predictors.
numbers: Odds ratios not read this session (abstract only).
limits: Abstract only. Correlational: strategy is not randomised, so hard cases may force hypothetico-deductive use.
agent_relevance: Strategy-to-accuracy link is confounded by difficulty. Do not hard-code one direction as a fix.

source: Coderre et al. (2004) The impact of two multiple-choice question formats on problem-solving strategies used by novices and experts
finding: Experts used scheme-inductive or pattern recognition about 90% of the time. Novices used them over 50% of the time, so novices also used expert-type methods often. Hypothetico-deductive use rose on the hardest cases for both groups.
numbers: 20 experts, 20 non-experts, 4 presentations, 2 formats. Expert hypothetico-deductive 5 of 80 per format. Non-expert 37 of 80 (MCQ) and 32 of 80 (EMQ). Expertise effect on expert-type process 2.69 (1.64-3.75, log-odds scale). Judge agreement 0.84. Format had no effect (p=0.31).
limits: Small N, gastroenterology only. Experts were gastroenterologists on a metabolic case where they were less expert and shifted strategy.
agent_relevance: Strategy depends on the case being hard for the solver, not only on the person. Supports switching mode on difficulty rather than a fixed rule.

source: Bass, Geddes, Wright, Coderre, Rikers, McLaughlin (2013) Experienced physicians benefit from analyzing initial diagnostic hypotheses
finding: Forced analysis of an initial hypothesis nearly doubled accuracy in nephrologists and residents. Scheme-inductive priming helped residents but made no difference for experts.
numbers: 9 nephrologists, 6 residents, 10 cases. Accuracy 31.1% to 65.6% (nephrologists), 40.0% to 70.0% (residents). Initial hypothesis accuracy 34.7%. 35% of diagnoses changed, 96% of changes wrong-to-right. Residents: scheme-inductive OR 5.69 (1.59-20.33). Nephrologists OR 0.57 (0.23-1.39). Experts failed to produce a scheme in 70% of scheme-primed cases.
limits: Very small sample. Priming compliance differed by group. Residents, not novices.
agent_relevance: Strong support for a generate-then-check loop: fast first hypothesis, then analyse it against the remaining data. Direction of the check mattered little for experts.

source: Norman, Sherbino, Dore et al. (2014) The etiology of diagnostic errors: a controlled trial of System 1 versus System 2 reasoning
finding: Telling residents to be slow and reflective did not improve accuracy over telling them to be fast.
numbers: Residents n=96 (Speed, 2010) and n=108 (Reflect, 2011), 20 cases. Accuracy 44.5% vs 45.0%. Time 69 s vs 89 s per case.
limits: Abstract only. Cohorts differ by year, not randomised in parallel.
agent_relevance: A generic think-slower instruction is not a useful operator. Specific moves (list alternatives, test the first hypothesis) are needed.

source: Singapore dental radiology trial (2022): ORAD DDx forward-reasoning aid vs Radiographic Atlas backward-reasoning aid
finding: Novice dental students did better with the non-analytic, diagnosis-first Atlas than with the feature-first forward tool. The forward tool did not beat control.
numbers: 99 third-year students in 3 groups, 2 cohorts. Mean improvement: Atlas 3.86, ORAD 1.99, Control 1.24. Atlas vs ORAD d=0.714 (p=0.014). Atlas vs Control d=0.997. ORAD vs Control p=0.769. In the ORAD group 80 of 152 post-test errors came from choosing a filter that excluded the right answer.
limits: Cohort 2 had COVID disruption. Cohort 2 group difference alone was p=0.064. Visual task, novices, not text reasoning.
agent_relevance: Feature filtering (forward) fails when one wrong feature rejects the truth. Agents should avoid hard exclusion on a single finding.

source: Norman, Brooks, Colle, Hatala (1999) The benefit of diagnostic hypotheses in clinical reasoning: instructional intervention for forward and backward reasoning
finding: Cited in the dental trial as showing that a diagnosis-directed (backward) approach beat a feature-based (forward) approach for novices learning ECG reading. Not opened.
numbers: Numbers not verified this session.
limits: Known only through citation in the 2022 Singapore paper and the Pelaccia reference list.
agent_relevance: Historic counter-example to the idea that forward is always better for novices. Confirm before use.

source: Patel and Groen (1986) Knowledge based solution strategies in medical reasoning
finding: Founding study. Not opened: publisher blocked access (HTTP 403). Commonly summarised as: experts who got the case right used forward (data to hypothesis) reasoning, and backward reasoning showed up in errors and less familiar cases.
numbers: Exact N and counts not verified this session.
limits: Statement is from background knowledge of the field, not from reading the paper.
agent_relevance: Background anchor only. Later work ties forward reasoning to case familiarity.

source: Khan, Mahboob, Ahmad (2022) Diagnostic errors: level of expertise, time taken and differential diagnosis checklists
finding: Maxillofacial trainees: training level was linked to error rate; time allowed and checklists were also tested.
numbers: 36 first-year and 36 fourth-year trainees; 15 vs 30 min groups; checklist vs none. Effect sizes not read.
limits: Abstract only, truncated. Written scenarios.
agent_relevance: Low weight.

source: Kaemmer, Schauber, Hautz, Stroben, Hautz (2021) Differential diagnosis checklists reduce diagnostic error differentially: a randomised experiment
finding: A checklist containing the correct diagnosis raised accuracy. A mere prompt to list alternatives did not. A checklist missing the correct diagnosis did not help and may have hurt.
numbers: 90 advanced medical students, 6 cases, 4 arms. Accuracy 0.75 (SD 0.44) with correct-containing checklist vs 0.49 (0.50) control. Own list contained the truth: prompt 0.69, DDXC+ 0.89, DDXC- 0.66 (DDXC+ vs prompt p=0.002). Mean rank of the correct diagnosis: 2.57 prompt, 2.04 DDXC+, 2.42 DDXC-.
limits: Students, computer cases, one chief-complaint list.
agent_relevance: Generating alternatives alone is weak. An external hypothesis list helps only if it is complete, which matters for any retrieval-based hypothesis step.

source: Pelaccia, Sherbino, Wyer, Norman (2025) Diagnostic reasoning and cognitive error in emergency medicine
finding: Two readings of dual-process theory. The check-and-balance reading (System 2 corrects System 1) is not supported by research. A harmonious reading says both fast and slow processing draw on the same knowledge.
numbers: Narrative review, no pooled effect. Reference list includes Norman 1999 (forward/backward instruction), Alqahtani 2016 (time pressure), Monteiro 2015 (second look not enough), Sherbino 2012 (response time vs accuracy).
limits: Only the abstract and the reference list were read in detail.
agent_relevance: Argues against designing the scaffold as a slow bias-correction pass added on top of a fast guess.

source: Goh et al. (2024) Large language model influence on diagnostic reasoning: a randomized clinical trial
finding: Giving physicians an LLM did not improve diagnostic reasoning. The LLM alone scored higher than physicians with or without it.
numbers: 50 physicians (26 attendings, 24 residents), up to 6 vignettes in 60 min. Median score 76% (LLM group) vs 74% (conventional), adjusted difference 2 points (95% CI -4 to 8, p=0.60). LLM alone +16 points (2 to 30, p=0.03). Time 519 s vs 565 s.
limits: Does not measure forward vs backward reasoning. Physicians were not trained in prompting. Vignettes, not live patients.
agent_relevance: A model alone can beat human-plus-model, so the model's own reasoning structure is the thing to improve.

source: Healy, Kossoff, Lee, Hasford (2026) Human-AI collaboration in clinical reasoning: a UK replication and interaction analysis
finding: UK replication of Goh 2024. Physicians with LLM help scored below the LLM alone. Low LLM use per question was explored as a reason.
numbers: 22 UK physicians, 4 vignettes, 2 with LLM. Gap to LLM alone 21.3 percentage points. Other numbers truncated in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Within-subjects, small N.
agent_relevance: Replicates the pattern that tool access alone does not lift human diagnosis. Not about forward vs backward.

source: Cardiac arrest team leaders in virtual reality: cognitive task analysis of experts and novices (2025)
finding: Experts reported inductive reasoning (cues to hypothesis) and considered reversible causes earlier. Novices reported treating before assessing. Experts reported lower cognitive load.
numbers: 7 experts, 5 novices, 12 VR simulations, 250 cognitive processes coded. Median load 53 (experts) vs 80 (novices).
limits: Tiny N, cued recall after the fact. The paper calls expert reasoning inductive and novice reasoning deductive, a third usage of these terms.
agent_relevance: A third meaning of forward reasoning shows the label is unstable across papers.

source: Dental radiology (Baghdady et al. 2014), as cited in the 2022 Singapore trial: non-analytic vs analytic instruction
finding: Cited as showing that dental students told to use a non-analytic approach diagnosed better than those told to use an analytic approach. Not opened.
numbers: Numbers not available.
limits: Secondhand through the 2022 Singapore paper.
agent_relevance: With Norman 1999 forms a small body saying diagnosis-first beats feature-first for novices in visual tasks.

source: Cognitive zipper model of clinical reasoning (2020)
finding: Proposes that early inquiry modes use backward reasoning and hypothetico-deductive strategy, and late confirmatory modes use forward reasoning and pattern recognition. So direction changes within one case.
numbers: Qualitative model with six inquiry modes. No effect sizes in the section read.
limits: Qualitative interview study, not tested for prediction.
agent_relevance: A single case can start hypothesis-driven and finish data-driven. A scaffold should allow phase changes.

source: Meta-analysis (2026): AI compared with physicians in clinical reasoning
finding: Pooled LLM vs human clinical reasoning showed no significant difference.
numbers: 1609 vignettes. Binary accuracy pooled OR 0.65 (95% CI 0.38-1.12, p=0.12). Continuous scores SMD 0.08 (-0.19 to 0.35). LLM vs novices OR 0.62 (0.35-1.1), I2=0%. Heterogeneity high elsewhere.
limits: Vignette studies, mixed designs, high heterogeneity. Direction of reasoning not coded.
agent_relevance: No pooled evidence that LLMs differ on diagnostic accuracy. No LLM meta-analysis codes forward vs backward.

source: Waqas et al. (2026) Reasoning beyond accuracy: expert evaluation of expressed diagnostic reasoning in LLM outputs for pathology
finding: Four reasoning models had similar factual accuracy but different expressed reasoning style. Scores were highest for algorithmic and deductive reasoning and lowest for heuristic and pattern recognition.
numbers: OpenAI o1, o3-mini, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking, DeepSeek-R1. 15 constructed-response questions, 11 pathologists, 7,920 ratings (9.75% missing). Gemini top overall. Deeper reasoning went with lower conciseness.
limits: 15 questions only. Rates reasoning as expressed in text, not true process. Not a forward/backward test.
agent_relevance: LLM outputs lean to deductive and algorithmic style, the opposite of the expert pattern-recognition profile, yet accuracy is comparable.

source: Sim and Chen (2025) Critique of impure reason: reasoning behaviour of medical LLMs (eLife review)
finding: Review of how to evaluate medical reasoning models beyond accuracy. Lists failure modes such as anchoring on initial symptoms and chain-of-thought mismatch with the final answer.
numbers: No pooled numbers. The words forward, backward and hypothetico-deductive do not appear in a diagnostic sense. Notes that no medical equivalent of ARC exists.
limits: Review, secondary summary.
agent_relevance: Anchoring on first symptoms in LLMs matches premature closure in humans. Fits a check-the-first-hypothesis step.

source: Protocol (2026): REACT-AI process-oriented assessment of clinical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Protocol only. 12 conditions (6 models, standard vs extended thinking), 13 subdomains, human expert panel. No results yet.
numbers: 180 AI outputs in phase 1, 3600 in phase 2. 173 student scripts held sealed. Results expected winter 2027. Hypothesis: extended thinking lifts reflection and metacognition most.
limits: No data. Cannot be cited for effects.
agent_relevance: Test to watch: does extended thinking improve the reasoning process, not just the answer.

source: Monteiro et al. (2015) Reflecting on diagnostic errors: taking a second look is not enough
finding: Title only, from the Pelaccia reference list. Not opened. Suggests that a plain second look does not fix errors.
numbers: Numbers not verified.
limits: Title only.
agent_relevance: Second-look instructions alone are weak; compare Bass 2013, where a structured check helped.

source: Alqahtani, Rotgans, Mamede et al. (2016) Does time pressure have a negative effect on diagnostic accuracy?
finding: Title only, from the Pelaccia reference list. Relevant moderator (time pressure). Not opened.
numbers: Numbers not verified.
limits: Title only.
agent_relevance: Time pressure is a named moderator to test for any forward vs backward claim.

source: Study access note: Patel and Groen-line replications and Elstein-style studies not retrievable
finding: Search budget and API rate limits (WebSearch exhausted, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar rate-limited, arXiv 429) blocked retrieval of the 1990s replications (Patel, Arocha, Kaufman 1994; Rikers; Hashem). Titles seen in Crossref only.
numbers: Seen as titles: Patel, Groen, Arocha (1990) Medical expertise as a function of task difficulty; Patel, Arocha, Kaufman (1994) Diagnostic reasoning and medical expertise; Rikers et al. ECG study (1997).
limits: Gap in this file. Do not treat as a negative finding.
agent_relevance: Re-run later for the task-difficulty paper: it is the key boundary condition (forward reasoning fades on hard cases).

source: Sherbino, Dore, Wood et al. (2012) The relationship between response time and diagnostic accuracy
finding: Title only, from the Pelaccia reference list. Relevant to whether fast pattern-based diagnosis is less accurate. Not opened.
numbers: Numbers not verified.
limits: Title only.
agent_relevance: Pairs with Norman 2014 (speed vs reflect, 44.5% vs 45.0%): speed per se is not the error source.
